summary: Clarifies how IS-IS routers should handle TLVs they do not support or that are invalid, because the way the protocol treats them is key to its extensibility. Deployment experience showed inconsistent behavior despite explicit statements in existing specifications. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: A router often receives a message part it doesn't understand. This document spells out what to do: skip over it politely, so new features can be added without breaking old equipment.

subtitle: Spells out what an IS-IS router must do with TLVs that are not allowed or not valid in a PDU.

tldr.problem: IS-IS is extended by defining new TLVs, but deployments behaved inconsistently when a TLV that is disallowed in a particular PDU, or invalid in some way, was received.
tldr.mechanism: Disallowed TLVs and sub-TLVs MUST be ignored, and a TLV with bad content MUST NOT cause the LSP carrying it to be rejected; LSP purges keep their stricter rules.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8918 makes the correct behavior explicit to maximize interoperability, adds no new protocol behavior, and fixes an error in the registry entry for the POI TLV from RFC 6232.

facts.label: Disallowed TLV in a PDU
facts.value: MUST be ignored; PDU not rejected

facts.label: Bad TLV content
facts.value: MUST NOT cause the LSP to be rejected

today: RFC 8918 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2020; the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It updates RFC 5305 and RFC 6232, so those documents are read together with its clarifications.

sections.title: Why TLV Handling Matters
sections.content:
The IS-IS protocol uses Type-Length-Value (TLV) encoding for all content in the body of its Protocol Data Units (PDUs). New extensions are added by defining new TLVs, and to keep this backwards compatible an implementation is required to ignore TLVs it does not understand. The same applies to sub-TLVs, which are contained within TLVs.

Equally essential is that validating a PDU is independent of validating the TLVs inside it. A valid PDU must be accepted even if one of its TLVs is not understood or is invalid, for example through incorrect syntax or an out-of-range value.

The RFC clarifies existing specifications to reduce non-conformant behavior seen in real-world deployments. It does not change the behaviors in existing specifications, but its clarifications serve as updates to RFC 5305 and RFC 6232.
sections.eli5: A letter has many paragraphs. If a router cannot read one paragraph, it should skip it and still read the rest of the letter instead of throwing the whole letter away.

sections.title: The TLV Codepoints Registry
sections.content:
RFC 3563 established the IANA-managed IS-IS TLV Codepoints Registry, whose initial contents were based on RFC 3359. For each TLV it records in which PDU types the TLV is allowed, using columns marked Y (allowed) or N (not allowed):

  • IIH: Hello PDUs, both point-to-point and LAN.
  • LSP: Link State PDUs.
  • SNP: Sequence Number PDUs, meaning PSNPs and CSNPs.
  • Purge: LSP purges, a column added by RFC 6233.

This registry is the reference for deciding whether a TLV is disallowed in a given PDU.
sections.eli5: There is a big list that says which kinds of message parts are allowed in which kinds of messages, like a rulebook for what may go in each envelope.

sections.title: Disallowed TLVs Are Ignored
sections.content:
The base IS-IS specification, ISO 10589, says that any codes in a received PDU that are not recognised shall be ignored. RFC 8918 says this is the model to follow for a TLV that is disallowed in the PDU where it arrives.

Therefore, a disallowed TLV in a PDU other than an LSP purge MUST be ignored and MUST NOT cause the receiving IS to reject the PDU itself.
sections.eli5: If a part is in the wrong envelope, do not panic. Skip it and carry on reading.

sections.title: Special Rules for LSP Purges
sections.content:
ISO 10589 recommends, but does not require, removing the body of an LSP before purging it, and accepts purges whose body TLVs are present, ignoring them. When cryptographic authentication arrived in RFC 5304, this looseness had to end so that attackers could not start a purge without the authentication key. RFC 5304 therefore said that ISes MUST NOT accept purges that contain TLVs other than the authentication TLV.

RFC 6232 extended this with the Purge Originator Identification (POI) TLV, and RFC 6233 added the Purge column to the registry to show which TLVs may appear in purges.

These stricter behaviors are not backwards compatible. The RFC 5304 behavior can only be safely enabled when all nodes support cryptographic authentication, and the RFC 6232 extensions only when all nodes support them. When new behavior is not backwards compatible, implementations are RECOMMENDED to provide controls for enabling it, to avoid interoperability problems and allow non-disruptive introduction.
sections.eli5: A cancellation notice is held to stricter rules than normal mail, so nobody can fake one. Because stricter rules can confuse older routers, they should be switched on carefully with a control.

sections.title: Sub-TLVs Follow the Same Rule
sections.content:
RFC 5305 introduced sub-TLVs, which are TLV tuples inside the body of a parent TLV. Registries for sub-TLVs are associated with the TLV Codepoints Registry and say in which TLVs each sub-TLV is allowed.

RFC 8918 updates Section 2 of RFC 5305 in two ways. It adds the sentence that sub-TLVs that are disallowed MUST be ignored on receipt. It also replaces the sentence 'Unknown sub-TLVs are to be ignored and skipped upon receipt' with 'Unknown sub-TLVs MUST be ignored and skipped upon receipt', which turns the statement into an RFC 2119 requirement.
sections.eli5: The same rule applies to the smaller parts tucked inside a part: if you cannot use one, skip it.

sections.title: Correcting the POI Registry Entry
sections.content:
RFC 6232 contained an error. Its Section 3 says the POI TLV SHOULD be found in all purges and MUST NOT be found in LSPs with a non-zero Remaining Lifetime, yet its IANA section says the values should be IIH:n, LSP:y, SNP:n and Purge:y. The correct setting for LSP is n.

RFC 8918 corrects this and also rewords the quoted text from Section 3 of RFC 6232: the POI TLV SHOULD be sent in all purges and MUST NOT be sent in LSPs with a non-zero Remaining Lifetime. In the IANA considerations, the registry entry becomes IIH:n, LSP:n, SNP:n and Purge:y, and its reference points to this document.
sections.eli5: One line in an older rulebook contradicted another line. This document fixes it so both say the same thing.

sections.title: Bad TLV Content Must Not Reject the LSP
sections.content:
The documents that introduce each TLV define its format, and the definition MUST also say what to do when the format or content does not conform, for example 'MUST be ignored on receipt'. A node that uses the information in a TLV or sub-TLV MUST verify that it conforms, including cases where the length is incorrect or the value breaks the defined restrictions.

However, the unit of flooding in the IS-IS Update process is the LSP. A TLV or sub-TLV with non-conforming content MUST NOT cause the LSP itself to be rejected. The RFC warns that failing to follow this results in inconsistent LSP databases on different nodes, which compromises the correct operation of the protocol.

LSP acceptance rules come from ISO 10589, with purge rules extended by RFC 5304, RFC 5310 and RFC 6233. The behavior when an LSP is not accepted is not altered by these extensions: whatever the reason for rejection, the Update process takes the same action.
sections.eli5: If one sentence in a shared notice is garbled, every router should still pass the whole notice along. Otherwise some routers would have the notice and others would not, and they would disagree.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the document makes no changes to the protocol, it introduces no new security issues. Its clarifications are meant to make it less likely that implementations process received LSPs incorrectly, which in turn makes it less likely that a bad actor could exploit a faulty implementation.

Security concerns for IS-IS are discussed in ISO 10589, RFC 5304 and RFC 5310.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is added, so nothing new can go wrong. Clearer rules just mean fewer mistakes for troublemakers to take advantage of.
